To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in both the United States and in Kenya, parents who had talked to their pre-teens about HIV/AIDS were more likely to be parents who perceived their child to ready to learn about sexuality, who had gotten information to help educate their pre-teen, and who had greater sexual communication skills, comfort, and self-efficacy.

Parent-child communication about HIV/AIDS is associated with parents’ perceived readiness of their child to learn about sex issues, the parent’s access to information to educate their children about sexual issues, and the parent’s sexual communication responsiveness (i.e., skill, comfort, and self-efficacy communicating about sexuality).

Parent–child communication about sexuality is associated with parents’ perceived readiness of their child to learn, their access to accurate information, and their sexual communication responsiveness.
